title: CSQ Unit 1 · Think Like a Robot (6-8)

items.q: A plan for a program written in plain words, step by step, is…
In a flowchart, a diamond shape means…
Which is pseudocode?
choices: Drive to the first gem and pick it up
a list of last week's scores
items.why: Pseudocode is a plan written as steps in plain words a person can read. A drawing, a photo or a list of scores is not a plan of steps.

items.q: Why write a plan (pseudocode or flowchart) before programming?
choices: because the game refuses to run
to think the steps through before building
items.why: Planning first means the hard thinking happens before the building, so the program is easier to get right.

items.q: Splitting a long route into "Drive to the first gem and pick it up", "Turn and drive up to the second gem", "Turn toward the goal and drive there" is…
items.why: Splitting one big route into smaller named parts is decomposing: each part can be built and tested on its own.

items.q: A loop inside another loop is a…
How many squares does repeat 3 { repeat 2 { move } } take Bolt?
items.why: The inside repeat runs 2 moves, and the outside repeat runs it 3 times: 3 times 2 is 6.

items.q: repeat 4 { move, repeat 2 { pick up } }: how many pick-ups?
items.why: Each trip around the outside loop picks up 2, and it goes around 4 times: 4 times 2 is 8.

items.q: Bolt must cross 3 rooms, each 4 squares long, turning right at each door. Which program does it with the fewest blocks?
choices: twelve move blocks and three turns
items.why: One nested repeat does all three rooms: 4 moves and a turn, three times over, in very few blocks.

items.q: A condition joined with AND, OR or NOT is a…
The door opens if Bolt has the key AND is touching the door. Bolt has the key, two squares away. Opens?
choices: no, both parts must be true
items.why: AND needs both parts true at once. Having the key is only one part; Bolt must also be at the door.

items.q: "if NOT wall ahead: move". When does Bolt move?
choices: when there is a wall ahead
when there is no wall ahead
items.why: NOT flips the answer. Bolt moves when 'wall ahead' is false, that is, when no wall is there.

items.q: Which program can reach the goal in a maze you have not seen before, without bumping a wall?
choices: move, move, turn left, move, move, turn right
repeat until goal { if path ahead: move, else: turn left }
if path ahead: move, else: turn left
items.why: In an unseen maze the program must keep checking as it goes. A fixed list of moves only works on a maze you already know.

items.q: A variable that holds only true or false is a…
Which is the clearest name for the number of gems left?
items.why: A clear name says what the box holds. gemsLeft tells a reader exactly what the number means.

items.q: Which type fits "is the door locked?"
items.why: Locked or not locked has exactly two answers, so a true/false flag fits it.

items.q: energy is 10. "change energy by -2" runs three times. What is energy?
items.why: Each change takes 2 away from 10: 10, 8, 6, then 4 after the third run.

items.q: A named group of steps you can call many times is a…
Room(steps) is called with 3 and then 5. What is "steps"?
items.why: A value you hand to a procedure when you call it is a parameter: here, how many steps to take.

items.q: Why give a procedure a parameter?
choices: to make the procedure run faster
so it never needs a loop inside
so one procedure can do different amounts
so it can only be called once
items.why: A parameter lets the same procedure take different amounts, so one block covers many cases.

items.q: You decompose a level into three subgoals. What should your program have?
choices: three separate procedures, one per subgoal
three copies of the same steps
items.why: Decomposing means one procedure per subgoal, so each part can be built and tested on its own.
